extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and journalism students (especially those covering police, criminal, and civil courts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting court, police, and judicial proceedings for newspapers: how to select, shape, and present judicial material (criminal trials, civil suits, probate, municipal court items) so stories are accurate, fair, and interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of court news
rubrics_metrics.description: To give fair and accurate publicity to significant phases of the administration of justice is the obvious reason for the publication of court news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer's aim should be to direct the reader's attention to those details of the proceedings (1) that are significant to him personally, (2) that affect the interests of the community, and (3) that relate to the welfare of society as a whole. Publicity of punishment also tends to deter others from similar illegal acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid destructive sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Destructive, or anti-social, influences, opposed to the best interests of organized society, are found in those court stories — particularly those of criminal and divorce cases — that play up disgusting or scandalous phases of such trials in order to gratify the morbid taste of some of their readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not emphasize lurid, disgusting, or scandalous details merely for public titillation. Such treatment is anti-social and undermines the public interest value of court reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not 'try the case in the newspaper'
rubrics_metrics.description: Another evil connected with the newspaper's treatment of court news is the so‑called 'trying the case in the newspaper' by means of news stories and editorials published before or during a trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid publishing and arguing evidence in ways that attempt to prove innocence or guilt outside the courtroom; do not print material that would be excluded under rules of evidence if doing so will create public opinion or prejudice that prevents the accused from receiving a fair trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of material: find and present significant matters clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: To find matters of general significance and interest, particularly when they are buried in legal technicalities and verbiage, and to present them clearly and attractively without sacrificing accuracy, are the main problems in handling court news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The body of court news stories usually consists of summaries of arguments, decisions, testimony, or legal documents, or of excerpts from them, with the necessary connective material. Emphasize salient and significant phases so routine matters can still interest casual readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead selection (feature choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead is usually determined by the status of the case. Any one of the important points may be made the feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the most newsworthy or consequential point (verdict, sentence, significant testimony, legal decision, human-interest angle, etc.) as the lead depending on what stage or status the case is in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony formats for news stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony in news stories is given in one of three forms:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) the question indicated by 'Q' and the answer by 'A,' both question and answer given in one paragraph without quotation marks; (2) the question and the answer in quotation marks, each followed by the necessary explanatory matter and each in a separate paragraph, like verbatim conversation in fiction; (3) a summary of the testimony of each witness in indirect quotation form, with the name of the witness at or near the beginning of the first sentence of the summarized testimony. Use the form that best fits clarity, brevity, and the publication's style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of a court story — essential items to include
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include as appropriate: (1) the verdict and the conditions under which it was rendered, (2) the sentence imposed, (3) the decision rendered and its significance, (4) important testimony, (5) net results of the day's proceedings in a trial, (6) the history of the case or action, (7) provisions of a will, (8) liabilities, assets, and cause in bankruptcy, (9) the award, or finding, (10) the grounds on which a suit is based. Select and present the subset relevant to the story's focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use human-interest elements where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal and civil cases often have a strong human interest element that, if rightly developed, may be a valuable part of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop human-interest angles (little comedies and tragedies of police court, personal backgrounds, effects on families) to make court stories appealing without sacrificing accuracy or fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize legal documents and technicalities faithfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the variety of material presented by different kinds of court news, it is difficult to indicate specifically the points to be considered in each story. To find matters of general significance and interest, particularly when they are buried in legal technicalities and verbiage, ... present them clearly and attractively without sacrificing accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using excerpts or summaries from legal documents, paraphrase technical language into clear, plain English while preserving meaning; avoid introducing interpretation that changes legal effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the appropriate story form for routine versus significant cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Since much court news is of a routine character, the matter-of-fact informative news story is a frequent medium for presenting it. This does not imply that such news is necessarily dry and uninteresting, for by bringing out salient and significant phases ... the facts of the news can be made of interest even to the casual reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use straightforward informative style for routine proceedings; use more developed narrative, background, or human-interest treatment for cases with broader significance or appeal, while maintaining accuracy and fairness.
